analysis_unit.subset_label: Yellow report style across pooled oncology comments
analysis_unit.notes: This corpus appears to pool positive and negative comments about the Yellow AI-generated report format across multiple oncology vignettes/scenarios rather than a single participant or single case.

summary.overall_impression: The Yellow report style was commonly valued for being concise, well organized, easy to scan, and clinically practical. Participants repeatedly praised its headings, bolding, tables, and patient-specific framing, especially when it translated evidence into actionable recommendations or monitoring steps. The main weaknesses were insufficient visibility and specificity of evidence, especially when citations were numeric, grouped at the end, or lacked hard data from studies. A recurrent tension was that the report was often seen as appropriately concise, yet some respondents still found it too long, too text-dense, or not sufficiently nuanced in how it connected data to recommendations.
dominant_negative_themes: Citations and evidence support were not transparent enough
Insufficient hard data or study detail
At times too long, dense, or overly definitive
dominant_improvement_requests: Make evidence support more explicit in-line with named sources and key results
Add more concrete trial data, study details, and evidence hierarchy
Improve practical linkage between data, recommendation, and patient application

positive_features.description: Many comments described the report as short, to the point, and appropriately sized for clinical review, with concise language that reduced friction in reading.
representative_examples: easy to read, short and concise

positive_features.description: Respondents frequently praised the structure, including headings, subsections, logical flow, and section-by-section breakdown that made the report easy to navigate.
representative_examples: great section-by-section breakdown with logical flow

positive_features.description: Formatting elements such as bullets, bolding, line separation, and tables were often seen as improving scanability and emphasis of key concepts.
representative_examples: bullet format with bold text to highlight key concepts
table was very helpful to draw a visual comparison

positive_features.description: The writing style was often described as plain, clear, and easy to digest without feeling condescending or visually distracting.
Participants liked when the report translated evidence into practical treatment, monitoring, dosing, or follow-up guidance relevant to actual patient care.
representative_examples: lists monitoring strategies which is helpful

positive_features.description: Comments valued the inclusion of patient factors, preferences, alternative strategies, and framing that made recommendations feel individualized rather than generic.
representative_examples: gives treatment options based on patient preference
the application to the patient is helpful

positive_features.description: Some respondents appreciated summary paragraphs, evidence summaries, risk-benefit framing, and comparison tables that condensed complex options.
representative_examples: compared the regimens at the end

positive_features.description: Several comments noted the presence of guidelines, NCCN references, and seemingly strong or reputable source material.
representative_examples: high quality sources from major organizations

negative_features.description: A dominant criticism was that citations were hard to use in real time because they were numeric, placed at the end, not hyperlinked, or not clearly tied to specific claims.
representative_examples: have to jump back and forth
sources aren’t written out after each fact it’s just a number

negative_features.description: Many respondents wanted more numerical results, direct study details, named trials, and clearer presentation of primary data rather than general statements.
representative_examples: lack of specific numbers/data from clinical trials
Should discuss studies and data more

negative_features.feature_label: Too long or text-dense for some users
negative_features.description: Although others praised its brevity, a substantial subset still experienced the report as too long, wordy, repetitive, or composed of dense text blocks.
representative_examples: Too wordy compared to amount of primary data

negative_features.feature_label: Weak connection between evidence and recommendation
negative_features.description: Some comments suggested the report did not adequately show how evidence supported the final recommendation or did not get quickly enough to the core clinical question.
representative_examples: does not get at core clinical question until the risk / benefits table
unclear where the evidence is coming from
Could use a bit more improvement connecting the data to the recommendations

negative_features.feature_label: Overly definitive or insufficiently nuanced language
negative_features.description: Several respondents were concerned that the report sometimes sounded too confident, insufficiently uncertain, or too one-directional in settings where nuance mattered.
representative_examples: Gives 'most appropriate' recommendation when multiple are appropriate

negative_features.feature_label: Gaps in completeness or relevance of evidence
negative_features.description: Some criticism focused on missing guidelines, sparse citations, unclear evidence strength, irrelevant references, or incomplete discussion of the most clinically relevant population.
representative_examples: citation list is on the shorter side
Citations seem to be for patients with follicular lymphoma

negative_features.feature_label: Variable usefulness of tables and summaries
negative_features.description: While some liked tables, others found summary tables poorly organized, redundant, pointless, or difficult to interpret.
representative_examples: Summary section poorly organized as a table

negative_features.description: A few comments raised worries about unsafe recommendations, logical errors, hallucinated patient problems, or ambiguity in dosing recommendations.

improvement_requests.description: Participants wanted citations to be embedded more transparently in the text, with named sources or clearer claim-to-source linkage rather than end lists or bare numbers.
representative_examples: Prefer named sources in-line w/ text rather than numbers
would like direct text from references
standard citation format would be better
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Opaque citation linkage and difficulty assessing source credibility while reading

improvement_requests.request_label: Add more hard data and trial specifics
improvement_requests.description: Respondents wanted concrete numbers, study outcomes, named trials, and more explicit discussion of what the cited evidence actually showed.
representative_examples: lack of specific numbers/data from clinical trials
would prefer to have outcomes of quoted studies presented as well
provide more information regarding the most relevant citations
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Insufficient primary data and limited trust in evidence summaries

improvement_requests.description: Several comments asked for better indication of whether evidence came from guidelines, randomized studies, or weaker literature, and for clearer ranking of citation strength.
representative_examples: details on if evidence is randomized or not would be appreciated
helpful to know what level of confidence, evidence the AUA is citing
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Unclear strength and relevance of supporting evidence

improvement_requests.request_label: Link recommendations more directly to patient care
improvement_requests.description: Participants wanted clearer explanation of how evidence translates into a practical recommendation for the actual patient, including shared decision-making and patient-facing language.
representative_examples: lack of a practical approach for how this info can be directly used for your patient
lack of practical language to share with patient
focus on population of patients who are relevant
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Weak evidence-to-action bridge and limited workflow usefulness in some reports

improvement_requests.request_label: Reduce text density while preserving substance
improvement_requests.description: Some respondents wanted the report tightened or reformatted to avoid long blocks of text, repetition, and unnecessary sections while retaining core evidence.
representative_examples: Graphically text was a bit dense
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Perceived verbosity and cognitive burden during review

improvement_requests.description: Comments suggested improving table design, adding separating lines, or using graphics more selectively so summaries add value rather than confusion.
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Inconsistent usefulness of current summary tables and visual presentation

improvement_requests.description: Participants wanted more balanced language in situations with multiple acceptable options, uncertainty, or risk-sensitive recommendations.
representative_examples: not very clear in any one direction
improvement_requests.targeted_problem: Overconfident tone and reduced trust in complex decisions

mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.theme_label: Concise for some, too long for others
mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.description: The same report style was described by many as ideal in length and by others as too long or text-heavy, suggesting differing thresholds for acceptable detail.

mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.theme_label: Tables as both strength and weakness
mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.description: Tables and summaries improved scanability for some readers but felt redundant, poorly organized, or unhelpful to others.
representative_examples: table was very helpful to draw a visual comparison

mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.theme_label: Concise summaries can aid workflow but weaken evidentiary trust
mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.description: Brevity and readability were appreciated, yet some readers felt this came at the cost of study detail, hard data, or nuanced evidence interpretation.
representative_examples: Vague and a bit too concise

mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.theme_label: Structured recommendations valued, but risk of sounding overconfident
mixed_or_tradeoff_comments.description: Respondents liked direct recommendations and practical plans, but some felt the report occasionally exceeded the underlying certainty of the evidence.

interpretive_notes: The strongest positive signal centers on workflow-friendly presentation: concise writing, visible structure, and practical organization appear to be central to the Yellow format’s appeal.

The strongest negative signal is not simple dislike of citations but dissatisfaction with how evidence is surfaced, linked, and quantified; respondents seem to want faster verification and more direct evidentiary grounding.
A key design tension in this corpus is that participants appear to want both brevity and richer study-level detail, implying a need for layered presentation rather than only more or less content.
Several comments suggest that trust depends not just on having citations, but on seeing what kind of source is being cited, what result it reported, and how that result justifies the recommendation.
data_quality_notes: The corpus is fragmented and pooled across scenarios, so themes reflect repeated sentiments across short comments rather than a unified narrative.
Some rows are non-informative or contradictory (for example, 'no data,' 'NONE YET,' 'perfect, no critiques'), and a few comments mix praise and criticism within the same fragment.
The subset appears to aggregate multiple disease contexts, so certain criticisms may reflect scenario-specific relevance issues rather than a universal property of the report style.
